questions.q: In which year did the English East India Company receive its royal charter from Queen Elizabeth I, and what was the charter's primary purpose?
questions.a: The charter was granted in 1600, giving the Company a 15-year monopoly on English trade with the East Indies. A wrong answer (e.g., 1613 or 1757) reveals confusion between the charter date, the first factory at Surat, and the Battle of Plassey — indicating the student cannot distinguish the Company's commercial origin from its later political conquest.

questions.q: Why did Mughal Emperor Jahangir grant a farman to the English in 1613 allowing them to establish a factory at Surat?
questions.a: Jahangir granted the farman because the English naval power could protect Mughal shipping from Portuguese pirates in the Arabian Sea, and the Emperor valued the customs revenue from English trade. A wrong answer (e.g., "the English defeated the Mughals" or "Jahangir wanted to convert to Christianity") shows the student misunderstands the mutually beneficial commercial-diplomatic relationship and overestimates early English military power.

questions.q: The English acquired Bombay in 1668. Explain how this transfer occurred and why it was strategically significant for the Company's expansion.
questions.a: Bombay was part of the dowry when Portuguese Princess Catherine of Braganza married England's Charles II (1661); Charles II leased it to the EIC for £10/year in 1668. Its deep natural harbor and location outside Mughal territory gave the Company a secure, fortified base independent of Indian rulers. A wrong answer (e.g., "won in war" or "bought from Mughals") reveals inability to connect European dynastic politics to Indian territorial changes.

questions.q: Compare the expansion strategies of the English East India Company and the Dutch East India Company (VOC) in India between 1600–1700. Identify two key differences in their approach to Indian rulers.
questions.a: The VOC focused on monopoly control of spice trade in the Indonesian archipelago, using military force to dominate Southeast Asian producers; in India they operated from Pulicat/Nagapattinam without seeking territorial sovereignty. The EIC, by contrast, sought Mughal farmans for tax-free trade, built fortified settlements with local permission, and gradually intervened in succession disputes (e.g., Carnatic wars). A wrong answer conflating the two shows failure to distinguish corporate strategies shaped by different commodity focuses and geopolitical contexts.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The English East India Company's transition from traders to rulers was inevitable once they obtained the right to issue dastaks (trade passes) in Bengal." Support your judgment with two pieces of evidence.
questions.a: The statement is partially valid but oversimplified. Evidence for: dastaks (from Farrukhsiyar's 1717 farman) allowed duty-free trade, which Company servants misused for private trade, depriving Bengal nawabs of revenue and causing friction (Murshid Quli Khan, Alivardi Khan). Evidence against: the Company remained subordinate to Bengal nawabs until 1757; Alivardi Khan successfully restricted European fortifications. Transition required the political vacuum after Alivardi's death and Siraj-ud-daulah's conflict with the Company. A wrong evaluation (fully agree/disagree without nuance) shows inability to weigh structural factors against contingent events.

questions.q: Create a timeline with annotations showing how the English East India Company converted commercial privileges into territorial control at three specific locations (Surat, Madras, Calcutta) between 1613–1700. Include the role of Indian rulers in each case.
questions.a: A strong timeline includes: 1613 Surat — Jahangir's farman after English naval help; 1639 Madras — Nayak of Wandiwash grants land for Fort St. George; 1690 Calcutta — Job Charnock negotiates with Subahdar of Bengal, later fortified as Fort William (1696) after Mughal permission. Annotations should show Indian rulers as active agents granting permission for strategic reasons. A poor timeline lists only English actions or omits the Indian ruler's role, revealing a Eurocentric view that ignores indigenous agency.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The English East India Company (EIC) established its first trading posts (factories) in India in the early 17th century, beginning with Surat (1613), and gradually expanded its commercial and territorial control through a network of fortified settlements, diplomatic ______ with Mughal and regional rulers, and military alliances, transforming from a trading corporation into a political power by the mid-18th century.
Fill in the blank: George in Chennai today — the first ______ fortress in India.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain the sequence and strategy of EIC factory establishment, analyze how trade privileges were converted into political footholds, and compare the EIC's expansion pattern with the Portuguese and Dutch approaches studied earlier.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: George in Chennai today — the first British ______ in India.
